Its aim is to build human resource capacity for strengthening decentralized health planning, especially at the district level, to improve accountability of health systems, elicit community participation for health, ensure equitable and accessible health facilities and to bring about convergence in programmes and services.

Introduction Rationale and scope The question confronting health systems in India is how best to reform, revitalize and resource primary health systems to deliver different levels of service aligned to local realities, ensuring universal coverage, equitable access, efficiency and effectiveness, through an empowered cadre of health personnel. One of the important prerequisites to achieving these outcomes is decentralized health planning to include conceptualization and operationalization of health programmes at local levels, as well as decentralized governance of systems of planning and delivery, at least at the level of the district. In India, a district is the smallest administrative unit. The country has 604 districts across its 28 states and seven Union Territories.

The district is considered the most appropriate level for operationalizing primary health. It is the basic unit of development, where agencies of various social development sectors, including health, plan and implement their programmes, thus providing a unique opportunity for integration and intersectoral coordination. The district provides an opportunity for interface between policy and implementation of health programmes at the level of the community, in addition to being a composite unit of the health system with a clearly defined administrative and geographical area – including the health subcentre (for 3000 to 5000 persons), the primary health centre (30 000 to 50 000 persons), the community health centre (80 000 to 100 000 persons), and the district hospital (catering to a population of about one million).

Districts vary widely according to the specific needs of their population, and even more so in terms of existing interventions and available resources. Strategies, therefore, must be district-specific, not only because health needs vary, but also because people's perceptions and capacities to intervene and implement programmes vary. In centrally designed plans there is little scope for such adaptation and contextualization, hence decentralized planning becomes crucial [1].

District health plans have also assumed a new centrality and urgency in the current context of the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM), 2005–2012, which was announced in April 2005 by the Government of India with the stated goal "to promote equity, efficiency, quality and accountability of public health services through community driven approaches, decentralisation and improving local governance". The NRHM includes decentralization of health planning to empower local governments to manage, control and be accountable for public health services as a core strategy [2].

The challenges For such planning to take place effectively, there is a strong need for trained, motivated, empowered and networked health personnel. But it is at this level that a lack of technical knowledge and skills and the absence of a supportive network or adequate educational opportunities impede personnel from making improvements. The limited nature of in-service training and of training curricula that reflect field realities add to this, discouraging health workers from pursuing effective strategies. There is also the need to evolve from a more "command and control" orientation of public health officials towards the community, to an attitude of participation, openness and accountability, recognizing the rights of the poor and the vulnerable. Capacity building is also needed in civil society groups, for members who are active in forums such as District Health Societies, district planning teams, hospital management committees and in the implementation of community health programmes.

One of the major gaps repeatedly identified by public health experts in the capacity of public health officials is the lack of experience and perspectives in the socioeconomic, cultural and political aspects of health and poverty [3]. Lack of capacity to analyse and interpret "what is really going on" in their area has led to an absence of district health planning and consequent outsourcing of this exercise to international technical assistance groups. This only propagates the situation of apathy and non-ownership on the part of the health officials.

Discussion The Public Health Resource Network Started in 2005, the Public Health Resource Network (PHRN) is an innovative distance-learning course in training, motivating, empowering and building a network of existing health personnel from government and civil society groups. Its aim is to build human resource capacities for strengthening decentralized health planning and to reach out to motivated, though often isolated, health workers. Thus, PHRN's objectives are as follows:

• reaching out to dedicated individuals to whom health equity is a major concern, and giving them access to essential information and opportunities to contribute to this goal;

• sharing public health technical resources with existing and potential district health programme managers towards strengthening the public health system in their districts, and assisting in the emergence of state and district resource groups for this purpose;

• empowering civil society to create spaces, and using the spaces being created under the NRHM, to improve and increase public participation in health planning and management;

• promoting decentralization and horizontal integration at district, block and village levels by building capacity in technical, programmatic, epidemiological and social understandings of health;

• strengthening the resource base needed for informed advocacy within the government and civil society;

• facilitating networking and mutual support among public health practitioners.

Structured as an innovative distance-learning course spread over 12 to 18 months of coursework and contact programmes, the PHRN comprises 14 core modules and five optional courses. The technical content and contact programmes have been specifically developed to build perspectives and technical knowledge of participants and provide them with a variety of options that can be immediately put into practice within their work-environment roles. The thematic areas of the course range from technical knowledge related to maternal and child health, communicable and noncommunicable diseases; programmatic and systemic knowledge related to health

planning, convergence, health management, and publicprivate partnerships; to perspective-building knowledge related to mainstreaming gender issues and community participation.

More specifically, the course covers the following main themes: Quarter 1 – Introduction to Public Health Systems; Reduction of Maternal Mortality; Accelerating Child Survival; Community Participation and Community Health Workers; Behaviour Change Communication and Training. Quarter 2 – Mainstreaming Women's Health Concerns; Community Participation; Disease Control Programmes; Convergence; District Health Planning. Quarter 3 – District Health Management; Public-Private Partnership; Legal Framework of Health Care; Issues of Governance and Health Sector Reform. Quarter 4 (Optional Courses) – Tribal Health; Urban Health; Hospital Administration;

Noncommunicable Diseases and Mental Health; Disaster and Epidemic Management. The PHRN now operates in the states of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Bihar and Orissa, with more than 500 participants. Initially supported by the State Health Resource Centre Chhattisgarh (SHRC), the PHRN is currently coordinated by the Public Health Resource Society (PHRS), which provides continuous support to the four state offices. The initiative has received valuable support from the NRHM at both central and state levels from state training institutes, the National Health Systems Resource Centre (NHSRC), and leading civil society organizations, including the Child In Need Institute (CINI), the Population Foundation of India (PFI) and the ICICI Centre for Child Health and Nutrition (ICCHN).

Besides the regular course, one other strategy of the PHRN is the fast-track capacity-building programme that is organized in collaboration with state governments willing to invest in their human resources. Such fast-track programmes have been organized in collaboration with the state governments in Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Chhattisgarh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura. Constructed as three rounds of a six-day-long training workshop held three to four months apart, this is focused on capacity building of government personnel working with NRHM for district-level planning. The goal is to build adequate skills in a team of about five resource persons per district for the next five years to create a pool of 25 public health officials from among motivated individuals from the government, from which a district resource unit can be made functional, to facilitate district health plans of good quality based on situational analyses, and to develop capacity to train panchayat (lowest unit of decentralized governance) officials and civil society groups in effective outcome-oriented village health planning [4].

Implementing the PHRN has contributed to valuable experience for establishing and sustaining a people's network, in close collaboration with the government, towards the end objective of building capacity to improve decentralized planning and programming. In terms of course participants, while the response to enrolment, contact sessions and the use of course material have been very encouraging, the challenge has been to motivate participants to undertake projects and assignments, especially due to the absence of any current formal accreditation. The collaboration of the government in organizing the fast-track capacity-building programmes and participation of the health system personnel have been positive, although follow-up of these concentrated sessions for translation into policy and practice must be strengthened. The cooperation of individual resource persons in volunteering for contact sessions and fast-track capacity-building programmes has made the decentralized operationalization of the PHRN possible.

Conclusion PHRN, independent of its capacity-building role, also must promote all interventions that would improve NRHM outcomes. To attain these larger goals, the PHRN has expanded its scope.

Two new initiatives of the PHRN are:

1. accreditation through the Indira Gandhi National Open University (IGNOU) for a postgraduate diploma in district health management. Participants who enrol in the course through IGNOU and fulfill the stipulated credits on the basis of course assignments and evaluations would be awarded the diploma.

2. to create and support a fellowship programme. The fellows supported through this programme would be placed in district health societies and local civil society groups, with strong and continuous mentoring support from a network of resource individuals and organizations from across the country. The envisaged role of these fellows is to support all community-level processes in the districts through advocacy, appraisal of training and community processes, formative studies for designing community programmes and improving training curricula, and documentation of ongoing processes.

An effort towards improving the PHRN has been an exchange of experiential learning with the distance-learning course for a diploma/master's degree in public health offered by the School of Public Health (SOPH) at the University of the Western Cape in South Africa. Sharing of course material between the two programmes, interaction with the SOPH to share opportunities and challenges of implementation and future directions, and conceptualiz-

ing partnerships in research have been valuable in strengthening the PHRN and planning for its future trajectory.

The PHRN is thus a network that responds to the unique needs of changing realities. It is an effort to build capacity and empower the participants to translate knowledge into action, and to bring about positive, equitable and sustainable change.

## Abstract

Pediatric high-grade gliomas (pHGGs) are among the most lethal childhood tumors. While therapeutic approaches were largely adapted from adult treatment regime, significant biological differences between pediatric and adult gliomas exist, which influence the immune microenvironment and may contribute to the limited response to current pHGG treatment strategies. We provide a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis of the pHGG immune landscape using single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics. We analyze matched malignant, myeloid, and T cells from patients with pediatric diffuse high-grade glioma (HGG) or high-grade ependymoma, examining immune microenvironment distinctions after chemo-/radiotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibition treatment, and by age. Our analysis reveals differences in the proportions of pediatric myeloid subpopulations compared to adult counterparts. Additionally, we observe significant shifts toward immune-suppressive environments following cancer therapy. Our findings offer valuable insights into potential immunotherapy targets and serve as a robust resource for understanding immune microenvironmental variations across HGG age groups and treatment regimens.

Keywords: immuno-oncology, tumor microenvironment, single-cell RNA-seq, pediatric high-grade glioma, tumor-infiltrating immune cell biology

## Abstract

LaBelle et al. show immune microenvironment changes following chemo-/radiotherapy and immune checkpoint blockade therapy via single-cell RNA-seq of matched tumor, T cells, and myeloid cells in pediatric high-grade gliomas (pHGGs). This study might help to explain the limited response of pHGGs to conventional therapies.

## Introduction

Pediatric high-grade gliomas (pHGGs) are the most common malignant brain tumors in children and young adults with limited treatment options and dismal prognosis. Therapeutic strategies, previously mostly adapted from adult glioma treatments, overlooked critical biological disparities across ages, including variations in driver mutations, mutational burden, and tumor cell states of distinct developmental origins, all together impacting the immune microenvironment.1,2,3 Advancements in understanding the latter and its interconnectivity of individual cell types through multiomic profiling have provided valuable insights in adult glioma and became instrumental for the prediction of treatment responses.4,5,6,7

Until very recently, studies reported on the deconvolution of immune cell signatures from bulk RNA expression data of pediatric brain tumors8,9,10,11 or utilized immunohistochemistry (IHC) and fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) analysis for immune phenotyping.12,13 These methodologies are constrained to a narrow spectrum of immune cell phenotype markers and lack the capacity to elucidate comprehensive single-cell interactions or the ramifications of treatments in pHGG. Few recent reports shed some light on the immune microenvironment of pHGG by single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). A study reported that microglia may induce mesenchymal transformation and T cell exhaustion in pHGG,14 but detailed information regarding treatment status and response to cancer therapy was lacking. Therefore, a deeper understanding of the specific immune landscape of pHGG is crucial for developing effective therapeutic approaches.15,16

To address this need, we sought to provide a more extended comprehensive transcriptomic profiling describing the pHGG-associated immune microenvironment, including infiltrating T cells and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), using spatial transcriptomics (10× Genomics’ Xenium In Situ platform), single-cell full length RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) (SMART-seq 2.0; SS2), and 5′ end scRNA-seq (10× Genomics scRNA-seq) techniques from fresh tumor samples collected from 27 pediatric patients diagnosed across different pHGG subtypes with detailed treatment information. We leverage this compendium to identify T cell and myeloid cell types and states, discern distinct immune cell states across patient age groups and tumor subtypes, as well as understand changes in these states before and after chemo-/radiotherapy or immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) treatment.

## Results

### A single-cell atlas of infiltrating myeloid and T cells in pediatric high-grade brain tumors

Our cohort reflects the clinical heterogeneity of the rare disease pHGG, encompassing samples across major molecular subtypes: diffuse high-grade glioma (HGG), H3-wildtype and IDH-wildtype (“H3WT_hemi,” n = 6); diffuse midline glioma (DMG) H3K27-altered (mutated: n = 9; altered: n = 1); diffuse hemispheric glioma H3G34-mutant (“H3G34RV,” n = 2); posterior fossa ependymoma, group PF-A (n = 7); and ZFTA/RELA supratentorial ependymoma (“ST-ZFTA/Rela,” n = 2). Due to their proposed radial-glia cell origin, ependymomas are classified as gliomas according to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification 202117 and are therefore included in this pHGG cohort. Overall, our cohort consists of 31 fresh samples from 27 patients (ages 0–18) profiled by full-length transcriptomic scRNA-seq (26 samples via SS2, as well as five samples profiled additionally via 10× Genomics scRNA-seq) (Figure 1A; Table S1).

Our cohort combines samples from patients who were either treatment naive at the time point of resection or biopsy (n = 15) or taken from patients after undergoing chemo- and radiotherapy (n = 12). Additionally, we collected longitudinal tumor tissues from two patients treated with ICI immunotherapy, who were diagnosed with diffuse HGG, H3 and IDH-wildtype (two recurrences per patient). None of our samples harbored a high tumor mutational burden (TMB), which we define as >20 mutations/mega base as recently described in the study by Patel et al. The highest detected TMB in a sample was 9.9 mutations/mega base (Table S1). TMB has been reported to impact ICI immunotherapy treatment outcomes and was recently analyzed in larger glioma studies.19,20

pHGGs are reported to exhibit an immunologically “cold” phenotype, i.e., presenting a low infiltration of immune cells, presumed to be a result of low mutational burden and reduced tumor antigen presentation.1,21,22 We first confirmed this phenotype by performing spatial transcriptomics on sections of four selected pHGG samples from our cohort (Figures 1B and S1A) with a combined pre-designed and custom-designed gene expression-targeting panel, including markers for human brain tumor and immune cells. Within each sample section, we detected <0.5% T cells and approximately 16% myeloid cells, confirming the “immunologically cold” phenotype typically observed in pHGG.

To overcome the observed low immune cell infiltration within our pHGG cohort for single-cell transcriptomics, we enriched specific populations by sorting fresh tumor samples per-operatively for immune cell-specific antigens by FACS (Figure 1C): T cells (cell viability dye Zombie NIR−, CD3+/CD45+), myeloid cells (cell viability dye Zombie NIR−/CD3−/CD45+), and other viable cells (cell viability dye Zombie NIR−, CD3−/CD45−), followed by scRNA-seq (SS2 or 10× Genomics scRNA-seq). Malignant cells were additionally identified from all viable CD3−/CD45− cells at a later stage with a computational approach combining copy-number variation calling and distinct clustering from a reference dataset for the annotation of non-malignant cells (see STAR Methods for details). Importantly, our overall approach included paired, matched sequencing for tumor and immune cells across all samples sequenced by SS2 (n = 24), allowing us to probe for communication networks between malignant, myeloid, and T cells.

After sequencing and quality control, we retained 3,178 malignant cells and 4,097 tumor-associated immune cells by using the SS2 protocol and 24,283 immune cells by using 10× Genomics scRNA-seq. Within all immune cells, we clustered and computationally annotated T cells (n = 2,698) or myeloid cells (n = 1,399) based on the expression of T cell (CD3G and CD3E) and myeloid markers (CSF1R), respectively. We also identified monocytes (marker FCN1; n = 149) clustering individually from myeloid cells (Figures S1B and S1C; Table S2). Following the annotation of major cell types, we separately analyzed individual transcriptional profiles of tumor, myeloid, and T cells to identify specific cell subpopulations. In addition to our newly generated pediatric cohort, we utilized published cohorts of adult tumor-associated immune cells (myeloid and T cells in adult glioblastoma [GBM] as well as IDH-mut5,23,24 and adult melanoma25) to characterize age-specific immune microenvironmental changes. For both myeloid and T cells, we processed the pediatric and published adult brain tumor cohorts by using the same experimental and computational approach.5,23,24 Tumor-associated T cells and myeloid cells presented with overlapping clusters, reducing the possibility of major batch effects between our pediatric cohort and published adult cohorts (Figure S1D).

Taken together, we present the largest cohort of paired tumor, myeloid, and T cells from matched patient-derived pHGG samples profiled by scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics. We next set out to investigate the different cell states and interactions among tumor-associated myeloid and T cells, while considering latest WHO classification subtypes,17 age, and treatment status.

### Deciphering myeloid cell programs and their intercellular interactome in pHGG

We next focused on tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells, as we and others have recently reported that myeloid cells constitute the major immune cell type for H3K27M DMG.2,26 Indeed, myeloid cells were the predominant immune cell type detected in our samples, as observed by spatial transcriptomics before as well as in our scRNA-seq dataset. In order to characterize all myeloid subtypes present within our pHGG cohort and their potential interactions with other cells within the tumor microenvironment, we performed non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) on the myeloid gene expression data of our pHGG cohort to detect programs, representing underlying cell states within all myeloid cells (Figures S2A and S2B; Table S2). We identified six myeloid-specific programs with the following annotations: hypoxic TAMs (hypoxic TAMs; markers: NUPR1 and TGFB1), interferon TAM (IFN-TAM; markers: IFI27 and IFI6), inflammatory TAM (markers: CCL2 and CCL4), microglia (markers: CH25H and EGR1), monocytes (markers: LYZ and FCN1), and SEPP1-high monocyte-derived TAM (SEPP1-Mo-TAM; marker: SEPP1) (Figure 2A). Annotation was based on overrepresented marker genes specific to reported myeloid cell states27 and was confirmed by analyzing program-specific genes for Gene Ontology term enrichment (Table S2). We validated all programs identified by NMF via 10× Genomics scRNA-seq (n = 3; Figures S2C and S2D; Table S3).

Of note, we identified a subset of CD3+ myeloid cells, characterized by concurrent expression of CD3E/D/G and myeloid markers such as CSF1R (Figures S2E and S2F). The number of genes detected in these cells did not vary from other myeloid programs, indicating that this cluster is unlikely to be a result of doublets. CD3+ myeloid cells have recently been described as likely pro-inflammatory within the central nervous system.28 We detected these cells in both the SS2 and 10× Genomics scRNA-seq data from our pHGG cohort, but not within the adult glioma datasets5 (Figure S2G).

To verify the expression of specific myeloid cell program markers at the protein level in tumor samples, we performed immunofluorescence staining on sections from H3 and IDH-wildtype diffuse HGG samples (Figure 2B). The markers were chosen based on SEPP1-Mo TAM (SEPP1), hypoxic TAM (LDHA), and IFN-TAM (IFIT3) programs. We indeed detected overlapping protein expression with IBA1 as a general myeloid cell marker. However, we also detect IBA1+ myeloid cells, which are negative for the respective marker (LDHA, SEPP1, or IFIT3). These results reveal the feasible detection of myeloid subpopulations, detected by their respective gene expression programs, on the protein level within the tumor microenvironment.

The existence of different myeloid cell programs and their respective subpopulations in pHGG suggests divergent functions in a cancer context-specific manner, as recently29 described. Therefore, we sought to determine whether specific subpopulations were overrepresented in particular pHGG subtypes. Surprisingly, we did not observe fundamental differences across molecular tumor types, but instead a heterogeneous distribution of the six different myeloid subpopulations across all samples, except for an observed enrichment of SEPP1-Mo TAMs in ependymoma samples and inflammatory TAMs in H3K27M DMGs (Figure 2C).

Next, we aimed to investigate whether our identified myeloid programs are derived from brain-resident microglia (microglia-derived TAM, Mg-TAM) or from bone-marrow-derived monocytes that infiltrate the tumor (monocyte-derived TAM, Mo-TAM, or monocyte cell types).30 Therefore, we categorized all myeloid cells from our pHGG cohort based on the six previously identified programs and scored them according to a reported marker gene signature for Mo-TAM, Mg-TAM, or monocytes27 (Figures 2D and S2H). As expected, microglia and monocytes were enriched for Mg-TAM and monocyte signatures, respectively. The cell programs SEPP1_Mo TAM and hypoxic TAM were enriched for the Mo-TAM signature, suggesting that the respective cell programs are composed primarily of infiltrating monocyte-derived cells/macrophages. IFN-TAMs were represented by both Mg- and Mo-TAM-derived signature scores, which imply that cells in these states putatively derive from either brain-resident microglia or infiltrating macrophages. Moreover, inflammatory TAMs exhibited a pronounced Mg-TAM signature score. Notably, we identified higher proportions of Mg-TAM-derived macrophages across H3K27M samples compared to other pHGG tumor subtypes (Figure 2E).

There is increasing evidence that myeloid cells drive distinct tumor cell states in adult GBM and affect the microenvironment through receptor-ligand interactions.6,31,32 To delineate inter-cell state communications in pHGGs, we performed CellChat analysis using the single-cell transcriptomic data, which pairs the expression information of cell type-specific ligands (“sender”) and their respective receptors (“receiver”), as previously described33 (Figures 2F, S2I, and S2J). Overall, the analysis suggested that myeloid cells predominantly engaged in ligand-receptor interactions with tumor cells, as well as showed preferentially more inferred interactions with CD4+ T cells than with CD8+ T cells. Within tumor cells, we identified increased inferred interactions with CD8+ T cells, while CD4+ T cell interactions remained comparatively underrepresented but also mostly interacted with tumor cells. Within the myeloid compartment, inflammatory TAMs primarily expressed ligands with receptors on major glioma cell subtypes: astrocyte (AC)-like, oligodendrocyte precursor (OPC)-like, and cycling tumor cells23,34 (Figure 2G). Conversely, these tumor cell types predominantly showed increased signaling to inflammatory TAMs, suggesting a potential signaling loop between adjacent cells.

Overall, we find a diverse landscape of six myeloid cell subtypes in our pHGG cohort, with no clear pattern across molecular tumor subtypes, except for an enrichment of SEPP1-Mo TAMs in ependymoma samples and inflammatory TAMs in H3K27M DMGs. Furthermore, SEPP1_Mo TAMs and hypoxic TAMs seem to be mainly derived from infiltrating macrophages, while inflammatory TAMs may originate from brain-resident microglia. Receptor-ligand analysis suggests that the latter may interact with AC-like, OPC-like, and cycling tumor cells, further supporting the hypothesis that brain-resident microglia might be involved in the progression and maintenance of pediatric brain tumors.35,36

### Deciphering pHGG-associated T cell states and their interactions in pHGG

Our spatial transcriptomic data revealed an overall small proportion of tumor-associated T cells below 0.5% across all pHGG consistent with prior findings.1,15 Using our method for cell enrichment from fresh surgical tumor specimen, we were able to significantly enhance our ability to study these underrepresented T cells at the single-cell level using transcriptomic analysis. In order to identify specific programs, which represent underlying cell states and subtypes within the T cell population, we derived de novo NMF T cell programs from our pHGG patient cohort as well as from previously published adult HGG-associated T cells5 (Figure S3A). Interestingly, we did not observe T cell clusters exclusively found in pediatric samples, suggesting a broad similarity between pediatric and adult cohorts at the T cell transcriptional level (Figure S3B). We next annotated pediatric tumor-associated T cell programs as follows: cytotoxic (markers: GNLY and GZMB), predysfunctional (markers: GZMK and HLA-DRA), cycling (markers: UBE2C and RRM2), interferon (IFN) response (markers: IFIT1 and IFIT3), memory (markers: CCR7 and selectin-L [SELL]), effector memory (markers: LMNA and NFKBIA), and activated effector memory (markers: TIMP1 and CRIP1) (Figure 3A; Tables S2 and S3). Within adult HGG-associated T cells, we identified two additional programs: Treg (regulatory T cells, markers: FOXP3 and CTLA4) and a stress-induced program (stress, markers: HSPA6 and HSPA1), but no IFN response program (Figures S3C and S3A). While Tregs, stress, and IFN response T cell programs were identified de novo only in adult or pediatric T cells, respectively, the low cell counts likely prevented program detection using NMF. To address this, we re-scored all adult and pediatric T cells for the nine programs and used these annotations as cell program assignments for downstream analysis. This resulted in the identification of 32 pediatric Tregs and 93 pediatric stress T cells, confirming that low cell count likely prevented program detection via NMF (Figures S3A–S3D).

We further investigated how these programs occur across tumor-associated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figures 3B, S3E, and S3F; Table S2). As expected, we identified cytotoxic and the predysfunctional program-associated T cell states only in CD8+ T cells, while Tregs were identified exclusively among CD4+ T cells.38 The remaining programs consisted of a mixture of both CD4+ and CD8+ subsets of T cells. We validated our findings and identified similar programs within the samples analyzed via 10× Genomics scRNA-seq (Figures S3G and S3K; Tables S2 and S3). The proportions of CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subtypes varied widely across our cohort (Figures 3C and 3D). Notably, we found high proportions of memory CD4+ T cells in ependymoma samples. Among CD8+ T cells, we observed a high proportion of predysfunctional program-associated and cytotoxic T cells for pHGG samples.

It has previously been reported that patient survival is correlated with an increased infiltration of CD3+ lymphocytes in pediatric brain tumors.12 Given the overall low T cell abundance in this pHGG cohort, we aimed to examine whether patient survival might be impacted by a distinct proportion of specific T cell states. We therefore analyzed a pediatric bulk RNA-seq cohort with associated survival data (ages 0–25 years old; n = 106; Children’s Brain Tumor Network [CBTN]).39 We leveraged our single-cell programs to deconvolute pediatric glioma bulk RNA-seq data and predict the proportion of each T cell program across each of the pHGG samples in that cohort. When correlating with survival data, patients with a high proportion of predysfunctional program-associated CD8+ T cells showed significantly improved survival (Figures 3E; Table S4). Additionally, high proportions of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells showed a trending beneficial survival impact, though not significant (p < 0.1) (Figure S3L). Patients with a low proportion of stress CD8+ and CD4+ T cells had a significant survival benefit. On the contrary, high proportion of IFN response CD4+ T cells was correlated with poor survival.

We next sought to investigate ligand-receptor interactions involving T cells and their tumor microenvironment. We found that CD8+ T cells exhibit a high degree of inferred interactions with tumor cells, particularly with AC-like, cycling, and OPC-like tumor cells (Figures 3F and 3G). In contrast, only few predicted interactions were shared overall between overall T cells and myeloid cells. Among those, CD4+ T cells mainly acted as “receivers” in myeloid cell signaling, primarily from microglia.

In summary, we describe a heterogeneous landscape of nine T cell programs across pHGG subtypes. Interestingly, we did not identify a dysfunctional T cell state with classical exhaustion gene marker expression (PDCD1, CTLA4, LAG3, and TIGIT), but rather found a potential predysfunctional T cell state.38 Notably, CD8+ predysfunctional program-associated T cells correlate with improved survival outcomes, while CD4+ IFN response T cells correlate with worse survival. Furthermore, CD8+ T cells and tumor cells are highly engaged in ligand-receptor interactions. In contrast, CD4+ T cells show less inferred interactions with surrounding cells and remain passive regarding ligand-receptor interactions with tumor or myeloid cells.

### HGG-associated immune cell populations reveal age-related diversities

After describing the pHGG-associated myeloid and T cell subpopulations, we next sought to further examine age-related differences in immune cell states. Among T cells, the same cell subtypes were observed across pHGG and adult HGG, although Treg and stress CD4+ T cells were detected at lower proportions in pHGG, while memory T cells (CD8+ and CD4+) and IFN response CD8+ T cell proportions were increased (Figures 4A, S4A, and S4B). We confirmed the finding for tumor-infiltrating Tregs and memory program proportions after correlating with age across our pediatric and adult HGG cohorts (Figure S4C). Interestingly, although proportions of T cells associated with dysfunctional and predysfunctional programs were comparable, program markers presented with increased expression in adult HGG-associated T cells (Figure 4B).

We next integrated all myeloid cell expression data from our pHGG cohort with published adult myeloid cell cohorts,23,24 which interestingly revealed age-specific differences in clustering, in contrast to the similarities seen for tumor-associated T cells across patient ages (Figure 4C). While we identified four myeloid-specific programs shared by pediatric and adult HGG samples (Figure S4D) (microglia, inflammatory TAM, monocyte, and hypoxic TAM), two myeloid programs were identified only in pHGG: IFN-TAM and SEPP1_Mo TAM. Two additional myeloid programs were identified only in adult patients: IFN Mo-TAM and transitory TAM (Figure S4E). Comparison of myeloid cell type proportions also revealed differences between pediatric and adult HGG: we detected significantly increased proportions of hypoxic TAM, IFN-TAM, and SEPP1-Mo TAM in pHGG compared to adult HGG (Figures 4D and 4E; Table S5). In contrast, in adult HGG, proportions of IFN Mo-TAMs were increased, and transitory TAMs were found exclusively in samples from adult patients. Inflammatory TAMs and microglia were highly upregulated in adult IDH-mutant HGG-associated myeloid cells, as previously described.23,40

We next aimed to quantitatively compare the degree of shared T cell and myeloid programs between pediatric and adult HGG. To assess this, we performed cell-wise correlation of matched T cell program scores (e.g., pHGG memory scores vs. adult HGG memory scores) as well as matched myeloid program scores (e.g., pHGG microglia scores vs. adult HGG microglia scores; Figure 4F). Interestingly, we found an overall higher correlation between adult/pediatric T cell programs than between adult/pediatric myeloid programs (83% of T cell programs and 50% of myeloid programs have Pearson correlation >0.75; Figure 4F). Overall, this suggests that, compared to the T cell population, the myeloid cell compartment may be more distinct between adult and pediatric HGG.

While we did not identify significant age group-dependent differences for T cells, we were interested in age group-specific clonal expansion of HGG-associated T cells, as recently described.41 Upon antigen recognition, tumor-reactive T cells can become highly proliferative (i.e., clonally expand). However, prolonged antigen exposure can drive upregulation of inhibitory checkpoint molecules, as we recently described for KLRB1 in adult HGG preventing T cell activation and leading to a (pre-)dysfunctional state.5,38,42 We therefore performed computational T cell receptor (TCR) reconstruction allowing for the identification of clonally expanded T cells but detected significantly fewer clonally expanded CD8+ T cells in our pHGG cohort compared to the adult cohort (Figure 4G). Furthermore, our analysis did not reveal significant expression of KLRB1 in clonal pHGG-infiltrating T cells (Figures S4F and S4H; Table S13). Instead, highly expressed genes in clonal T cells were cytotoxicity related (e.g., NKG7, GNLY, and GZMB).

Consequently, and given the observed overall low percentage of T cells infiltrating pHGG, we sought to identify checkpoint markers independent of their presence in clonally activated cells. To this end, we focused on genes with >100 counts across all cells and then correlated log1p normalized gene expression values with T cell program scores for each CD8+ T cell. We subsequently ranked genes in each program according to their Pearson correlation (Figure 4H). We then screened the top 100 ranked genes within the cytotoxic CD8+ T cell program for potential candidate targets (1) described in the literature as immune checkpoint and (2) being expressed on the surface to be therapeutically targetable. While here we indeed found KLRB1 in our pediatric pHGG cohort as highly expressed in cytotoxic T cells (but not in clonally expanded T cells, as described earlier), we also identified the gene SELPLG (protein name CD162, alias PSGL-1) (Figure 4H). This gene has been previously described as an immune checkpoint regulator preventing T cell activation, increasing T cell exhaustion, and inhibiting tumor infiltration in anti-PD-1-resistant melanoma.43,44,45 Interestingly, SELPLG revealed its highest expression in both pediatric and adult cytotoxic CD8+ T cells infiltrating tumors, compared to the other T cell states (Figure 4I). To validate SELPLG expression at the protein level on the surface of pHGG cells, we performed CD162 staining and FACS analysis of three freshly obtained pHGG samples. Our analysis indeed confirmed detectable CD162 expression on most T cells, which was also accompanied by detectable PD-1 expression (Figures 4J and S4I). Furthermore, we found the expression of its paired cell adhesion molecule, SELL, in naive T cells as well as monocytes (Figure S4J).

In conclusion, we identified potential differences in myeloid cell subpopulations between pHGG and adult HGG, suggesting distinct modulation of the immune microenvironment. However, we observed only marginal variance in T cell subpopulation profiles between adult and pHGGs, with the latter showing significantly less clonal expansion in pHGG. Finally, we identified CD162 as a highly expressed checkpoint molecule expressed on the surface of cytotoxic pediatric CD8+ T cells, which might open therapeutic avenues for immune-oncology treatment in pHGG.

### Cancer therapy affects immune cell proportions in pHGG

Conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy have been reported to modulate the composition of tumor-infiltrating immune cells in adult HGG.46 We therefore sought to address how the immune microenvironment changes in our pHGG cohort after treatment. To do so, we compared samples from treatment-naive patients with those who received chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy. Inflammatory TAMs and microglia were significantly reduced in patients who had received chemo-/radiotherapy, while other myeloid subpopulations remained unchanged (Figure 5A). This finding indicated a potential reduction of brain-resident myeloid cells after treatment. In tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells, we observed a significant reduction within the stress T cell population (Figure 5B), while the other CD8+ T cell subtypes remained mostly unchanged. Interestingly, within CD4+ T cells, we did not observe significant changes in proportions for chemo-/radiotherapy-treated samples (Figure S5A).

Initial studies in adult glioma indicated promising effects of anti-PD-1 neoadjuvant (i.e., prior to surgical tumor removal) treatment; however, recent clinical trials for the same immunotherapy approaches in pHGG populations have not demonstrated a survival benefit.47,48 We therefore sought to examine the composition of the tumor immune microenvironment in two patients with pHGG treated with ICI and compare them to immunotherapy-naive (ITN) patients (Figure S5B). Notably, we detected a significant increase in T cell infiltration in samples from ICI-treated patients, as had been previously reported for adult glioma49 (Figure S5D). However, even though most CD8+ T cell program proportions between samples from ICI-treated and ITN patients had not changed, we found a significant increase in tumor-infiltrating Tregs within the CD4+ T cell subpopulation, which are known to contribute to an immune-suppressive microenvironment50 (Figures 5C and S5C). We confirmed these finding by using multiplex IHC (Treg cell marker: FOXP3) on pHGG tissue samples (Figures 5D and 5E). Notably, we observed a significant increase of Tregs in the tumor samples of both ICI-treated patients. Moreover, while markers for dysfunctional, predysfunctional, and cytotoxic T cell states were overall lowly expressed in CD4+ T cells, they were upregulated in CD4+ T cells after ICI treatment, but largely unaltered in CD8+ T cells (Figure 5F). Expression changes of these markers in CD4+ T cells were less pronounced in adult HGG (Figure S5E). In contrast to the observed proportion changes in T cells after ICI treatment, we did not identify any differences in myeloid cells after treatment (Figure 5G). Interestingly though, we did observe myeloid cell proportion changes in the two ICI-treated patients, including an increase of hypoxic TAMs and a loss of microglia and inflammatory TAM subpopulations. This effect was similar compared to the impact on myeloid cells observed in generally chemo-/radiotherapy-treated samples.

We next aimed at gaining more insight into immunotherapy resistance in glioma. In contrast to both pediatric and adult gliomas, melanoma tumors have historically shown promising response to ICI, including anti-PD-1-targeted therapies.51 We therefore sought to compare tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cell states between glioma and melanoma. We integrated glioma CD8+ T cells from both adult and pediatric cohorts with a published melanoma CD8+ T cell SS2 dataset25 to enable a more direct comparison. We re-scored all cells for dysfunctional, cytotoxic, predysfunctional program-associated, and naive gene sets,27 revealing high concordance of these cell states across both tumor types (Figures S5F and S5G). Melanoma CD8+ T cells expressed dysfunctional markers markedly higher than glioma T cells (CTLA4, TIGIT, HAVCR2, and PDCD1; Figure 5H), suggesting increased susceptibility to ICI immunotherapy. In alignment with this finding, melanoma CD8+ T cells also contained a higher proportion of dysfunctional T cell subpopulation (Figure 5I). In contrast, we found elevated cytotoxic marker expression in glioma CD8+ T cells as well as a higher cytotoxic T cell subpopulation compared to melanoma CD8+ T cells (Figures 5H and 5I). In addition, melanoma samples did not reveal a significant increase in tumor-infiltrating Treg proportions within the CD4+ T cell population upon immune checkpoint blockade (Figure 5J).

In summary, our study reveals that chemo-/radiotherapy and ICI may affect cell type proportions within the immune microenvironment of pHGGs. Specifically, we observed a downregulation of pro-inflammatory compartments and an upregulation of anti-inflammatory components. If these findings are validated in a larger cohort, they would challenge the desired therapeutic outcomes in cancer treatment of this patient population.

## Discussion

In this study, we comprehensively profiled the immune and corresponding tumor cell landscape at single-cell transcriptome level across pHGGs, integrating myeloid, T cell, and tumor cell states. We reveal a remarkable divergence among myeloid cell state proportions between pediatric and adult patients. In contrast, we identified a high degree of similarity across T cell states of pediatric and adult tumor-associated T cells. This finding underscores that clinical studies conducted on adult gliomas may not always be directly applicable to pediatric cases, highlighting the critical need for pediatric-specific research. Further, our data provide significant evidence that chemo-/radiotherapy and ICI immunotherapy may alter the immune microenvironment, which equally will need to be taken into account when designing clinical trials for patients with relapsed pHGG.

Intratumoral cell-cell communication is an increasingly important and debated field in tumor biology, offering the potential for significant advancements in our understanding of how tumors manipulate and get manipulated. Recent reports from the emerging field of cancer neuroscience reveal that tumor cells are capable of interacting with neurons within the brain.52 Conversely, certain tumor-infiltrating immune cells have been reported to direct the fate of glioma cells into distinct states.6 Here, we uncover that AC-like, cycling, and OPC-like tumor cell states represent with the highest relative numbers of inferred interactions with inflammatory TAMs and CD8+ T cells based on respective ligand-receptor expression levels (Figures 3 and 4). Whether inflammatory TAMs promote or inhibit tumor growth in pHGG remains to be elucidated. However, the finding was partially consistent with our previous spatial transcriptomics work in K27M DMGs showing that differentiated AC-like tumor cells colocalize with immune cells.2 Interestingly, the MES-like tumor cell state, which we had previously found to be enriched for interactions with myeloid cells in adult K27M DMGs, was not observed to have such substantial interactions in our pHGG cohort.6 This is likely because of our purely pediatric age group examined here (oldest patient = 18 years). Interestingly, our data suggest that AC-like, OPC-like, and cycling glioma cells presented the major hub of local interaction with the environment. This aligns with studies reporting on differentiated tumor cells, including OPC-like and AC-like cells, that are able to communicate with the normal brain environment, like neurons, which contributes to overall tumor growth.53,54,55

In regard to our findings of therapy-induced differences of immune cell states and proportions, a previous study demonstrated that immune cell populations can be significantly affected following chemo-/radiotherapy in adult HGGs, showing an overall decrease in T and B cells, but an increase in tumor-infiltrating Tregs among CD4+ T cells.46 In accordance with these results, we observed alterations in the pHGG immune microenvironment after chemo-/radiotherapy. Specifically, we observed that proportions of inflammatory TAMs and microglia were significantly reduced after chemo-/radiotherapy, while other myeloid subpopulations remained unchanged (Figure 5A). This indicates a potential targeted impact on brain-resident myeloid cell types, as reported for adult glioma.56,57 The depletion or inhibition of these immune cell populations may benefit the anti-inflammatory tumor environment, which could impact overall anti-tumor immune responses and treatment outcomes. Further studies will be needed to elucidate the specific mechanisms underlying this observation and to determine the functional consequences of this myeloid cell subpopulation shift on tumor progression and treatment response.

In addition to the analysis of samples from patients treated with chemo-/radiotherapy, we investigated the impact of ICI immunotherapy on the tumor-associated immune cell proportions. A recent clinical trial using ICI immunotherapy treatment with nivolumab (anti-PD-1) has shown limited response in pediatric patients diagnosed with glioma.47 Our study provides potential mechanistic insights that may help explaining the limited response: (1) the immune microenvironment presented with high anti-inflammatory features after ICI therapy, compared to ITN counterparts, driven by infiltration of Tregs and a decrease in pro-inflammatory brain-resident myeloid cells. (2) The observed absence of CD8+ T cell exhaustion or activation, indicated by low exhaustion marker expression, stands in stark contrast to melanoma, which responds well to ICI.

Along with the primitive immune system in children,58 these findings highlight the complexity of the immune response in pHGG and underscore the need to consider the recruitment, activation, and retention of tumor-specific effector immune cells, as well as the co-targeting of cancer-specific vulnerabilities in the development of immunotherapy strategies for pHGG.16,59

KLRB1 was recently described as target for ICI immunotherapy in adult HGG.5 Our findings reveal lower clonal expansion of CD8+ T cells within pHGGs compared to adult HGG, suggesting an inability to mount an effective anti-tumor response and confirming potential challenges in antigen presentation or weak immune activity against the tumor.42 Instead, we identified SELPLG/CD162, a previously described immune checkpoint, as highly expressed specifically in cytotoxic CD8+ T cells. We hypothesize, given the reported function of CD162, that it could impact full activation of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells besides clonal activation. Studies in other cancers had suggested that CD162 inhibits T cell activation and promotes exhaustion upon binding to its paired adhesion molecules (selectins L, E, and P).43 Blocking CD162 via ICI may enhance anti-tumor immunity, T cell proliferation, and promote infiltration. Unfortunately, ICI immunotherapy has been shown to have limited effects in “cold” tumors.47 However, leveraging chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy recently demonstrated impressive efficacy in pediatric K27M DMGs.60,61 Given the high ubiquitous expression of CD162 on the T cell surface and the beneficial microenvironment for its stimulation, knocking out SELPLG on the CAR T cells, or antagonizing with a specific antibody, could enhance CAR T cell efficiency. Importantly, pre-clinical in vivo experiments have shown that SELPLG−/− mice showed a normal lifespan, their T cells have an increased anti-viral activity, and peripheral T cells remained unaltered, but the general cytokine expression in the blood was increased.43 Furthermore, in anti-PD-1-resistant melanoma mouse models, CD162 inhibition led to reduction of tumor-infiltrating Tregs.45

In summary, we present an extensive, comprehensive single-cell transcriptional map of the immune microenvironment in pediatric gliomas. It sheds light on the challenges faced in treating pHGG and highlights the differences in immune response compared to adult HGG. Furthermore, our findings offer valuable insights into potential immunotherapy targets. Serving as a robust resource, this study deepens the understanding of immune microenvironmental variations across different HGG age groups and treatment regimens.

### Limitations of the study

The study’s cohort size constrains our capacity to draw definitive, significant conclusions regarding immune cell proportions and interactions between patients. Further studies in a larger pediatric cohort that contains a more substantial number of each tumor subtype will be necessary to confirm our observations. Due to the limited number of anti-PD-1-treated pediatric glioma patient samples, additional patient samples from matched tumor type and age range will be required to more confidently validate our findings from this limited cohort. Additionally, further studies that include both pediatric and adult samples processed together will be required to completely eliminate the possibility of batch effects driving the age effects described in this manuscript. In addition, mechanistic experiments and functional validation in vitro and in vivo are essential to confirm the cell type changes and the identified immune checkpoint targets described in this manuscript and will be addressed in future studies.

### Experimental model and study participant details

#### Patients

27 pediatric patients were enrolled in the study. Patients were 0–18 years old, 11 Female and 16 Male, and they were diagnosed with diffuse high-grade glioma, H3-wildtype and IDH-wildtype (“H3WT_hemi”, n = 6); diffuse midline glioma (DMG) H3K27-altered (mutated: n = 9; altered: n = 1) diffuse hemispheric glioma (DHG) H3G34-mutant (“H3G34RV”, n = 2); posterior fossa ependymoma, group PF-A (n = 7); and ZFTA/RELA supratentorial ependymoma (“ST-ZFTA/Rela”; n = 2). All samples used in this study were deidentified and obtained with properly informed consent of patients and/or their legal representatives, who did not receive compensation. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at Boston Children’s Hospital/Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (DFCI 10–417) and by the Medical University of Vienna (EK Nr:1244/2016).

### Method details

#### Spatial transcriptomics with Xenium

#### Gene panel design

For Xenium In Situ analysis, we employed the human brain pre-designed panel containing probes for 272 genes encompassing additional non-malignant cell types (oligodendrocytes, immune cells, endothelial, astrocytes, neurons, microglia, and VLMCs). Additionally, a custom-designed gene panel of 100 genes includes marker genes identified across different types of high-grade gliomas, including: (1) H3K27M diffuse midline gliomas34 (n = 10 genes); (2) H3 and IDH wildtype gliomas38 (n = 27 genes); (3) ZFTA-RELA tumors (n = 35 genes); and (4) normal cell types (n = 18) (Table S11).

#### Sample preparation

Sample preparation was performed according to the 10x Xenium In Situ protocol. In brief, each sample previously fixed in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) blocks, was cut into 5 μm tissue sections and collected onto a Xenium slide, followed by deparaffinization and permeabilization. A mix of pre-designed and custom-designed gene expression probe hybridization occurred at 50°C overnight. After multiple washing to remove un-hybridized probes, ligation of probes and annealing of rolling circle amplification (RCA) primer occurred at 37°C for 2 h. Circularized probes were then enzymatically amplified at 30°C for 2 h, background autofluorescence was quenched chemically and nuclei were stained with DAPI. Xenium slide with the stained samples was then loaded into the Xenium Analyzer for initial run.

#### Xenium In Situ imaging

Image acquisition and sample handling was automated within Xenium Analyzer for two slides per run. 15 rounds of fluorescence probe hybridization, imaging, and probe removal occurred within the Analyzer. Fast area scan camera with ∼200 nm per-pixel resolution was used for image acquisition, and Z-stacks were taken with 0.75 μm step size across tissue thickness. All z stack of images were then processed and stitched, using DAPI image as reference. Each fluorescently labeled oligonucleotide bound to amplified barcodes was detected and registered in each cycle. Unique optical signature from fluorescence intensity over the 15 rounds was used to identify a target gene. For cell segmentation, neural network was used to detect each nucleus from DAPI images.

#### Single-cell isolation from tumor tissue via FACS

Tumor samples were mechanically cut into small pieces with a sterile scalpel and further dissociated into single cell suspensions using the brain dissociation kit from Miltenyi Biotec (Bergisch Gladbach, Germany) following the manufacturer’s protocol. Single cell suspension was filtered with a 70uM filter to remove cell clumps. Fc receptor blocking was performed on the total cell suspension using Human TruStain FcX reagent (Biolegend; San Diego, CA). Cell suspensions were subsequently stained for cell sorting using the following antibody panels: CD3-BV421 (Biolegend, 300434) as T cell marker, CD45-BV650 (Biolegend, 304044) as marker for Myeloid cells, and CD64-PE (Biolegend, 305008) as exclusion marker to distinguish T cells more specific from other cells. As cell viability dye, TO-PRO-3 Iodide (detects dead cells) or Calcein (detects live cells) were used. For all experiments, compensation was performed. For single cell sorting, we used a BD Biosciences Aria III or Sony MA900 fluorescence-activated cell sorter with a 100 μm nozzle.

Live, single T cells (gating: Calcein positive, CD45+, CD3+), Myeloid cells (gating: Calcein positive, CD45+, CD3+), and tumor cells (gating: Calcein positive, CD45–) from tumor samples were sorted into individual wells of a 96-well PCR plate (Eppendorf; Hamburg, Germany) that contained 10uL/well of TCL buffer QIAGEN; Venlo, Netherlands). Plates were immediately centrifuged at 800xg for 1 min at 4°C and frozen on dry ice. For 10X Genomics, 15,000 live, single T cells or Myeloid (gating: Calcein, CD45+, CD3+) were sorted in a 15mL Falcon tube containing 8mL media (RPMI).

#### scRNA-seq data generation

#### 10X genomics

The 10x Genomics cell suspension and library preparation, as well as sequencing was performed following the detailed manufacturer’s protocol.62 The isolated single cells (T cells, Myeloid cells, or tumor cells) were loaded into separate channels of a Single Cell Chip A with reverse transcriptase reagent mixture and 50ul gel beads according to the manufacturer’s protocol (10X Genomics; Pleasanton, CA). Chips were next loaded into the 10X Genomics Chromium Controller for single-cell partitioning, immediately followed by emulsion recovery from the chip and incubated in a deep-well block thermocycler for the reverse transcription reaction. cDNA isolation and library preparation were completed as per the manufacturer’s protocol. Isolated cDNA was amplified (13 cycles). Consecutively, cDNA was allocated for preparation of a gene expression library or TCR enrichment/library preparation with the Chromium Single Cell V(D)J TCR kit (10X Genomics). The quality of the cDNA and library was evaluated using the 2100 BioAnalyzer (Agilent). T cell gene expression libraries and TCR V(D)J libraries were sequenced on the Illumina Nextseq 500 sequencer with 150 bp paired-end read configuration. For gene expression libraries ∼50,000 reads per cell (median) and for TCR enriched libraries 175,000 reads per cell (median) were obtained.

#### Smart-seq2

Single cell whole transcriptome amplification and sequencing libraries were prepared using the adapted SMART-seq2 protocol as described in Mathewson et al..5 RNA was purified with Agencourt RNAClean. Oligo-dT primed reverse transcription (RT) was performed using Maxima H Minus reverse transcriptase (Life Technologies) and a template-switching oligonucleotide (TSO; Qiagen). RNase inhibitor was added to the dT annealing step at 1U/ml. Trehalose (1M) was used instead of water to fill up the reaction volume. For the reverse transcription step, Maxima RNaseH-minus RT (200 U/ml) was used as the RT enzyme at 2U/ml. MgCl2 was added at 1M and DTT was omitted from the reaction. Trehalose (1M) was used to stabilize the reaction. The RT step was performed at 50°C for 90 min followed by 85°C for 5 min. In the PCR pre-amplification step, an ISPCR primer was used at 0.2 mM and PCR was performed for 21 cycles using KAPA HiFi HotStart ReadyMix (KAPA Biosystems). PCR purification was performed using AMpure XP beads at 0.8X. Libraries were enriched with dual indexes using Illumina Nextera XT Library Prep kits. Libraries from 384 immune cells with unique barcodes were pooled together and sequenced at 2pM on an Illumina Nextseq 500 sequencer, yielding paired-end 38 base pair reads with 8bp indexes.

#### Tumor mutational burden detection

For DFCI tumor samples, Tumor Mutational burden detection is part of the OncoPanel performed at the BWH’s Center for Advanced Molecular Diagnostics (CAMD). OncoPanel is a cancer genomic assay to detect somatic mutations, copy number variations and structural variants in tumor DNA extracted from fresh, frozen or formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples. The OncoPanel assay surveys exonic DNA sequences of 447 cancer genes and 191 regions across 60 genes for rearrangement detection.

In brief, between 50 and 200 ng tumor DNA containing at least 20% tumor nuclei was prepared as previously described,19 hybridized to custom RNA bait sets (Agilent SureSelectTM, San Diego, CA) and sequenced using Illumina HiSeq 2500 with 2 × 100 paired-end reads. Sequence reads were aligned to reference sequence b37 edition from the Human Genome Reference Consortium using bwa, and further processed using Picard (version 1.90, http://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/) to remove duplicates and Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK, version 1.6-5-g557da77) to perform localized realignment around indel sites. Single-nucleotide variants were called using MuTect v1.1.439, insertions and deletions were called using GATK Indelocator, and variants were annotated using Oncotator40. Copy number variants and structural variants were called using the internally developed algorithms RobustCNV41 and BreaKmer42 followed by manual review. To filter out potential germline variants, the standard pipeline removes SNPs present at >0.1% in Exome Variant Server, NHLBI GO Exome Sequencing Project (ESP), Seattle, WA (http://evs.gs.washington.edu/EVS/, accessed May 30, 2013), present in dbSNP, or present in an in-house panel of normal tissue, but rescues those also present in the COSMIC database. Variants were further filtered by removing variants present at >0.1% in the gnomAD v.2.1.1 database or annotated as benign or likely benign in the ClinVar database44,45. Arm-level copy number changes were generated using an in-house algorithm specific for panel copy number segment files followed by manual expert review. We set a copy number segment mean log2 ratio threshold at which we could accurately call arm amplification and deletion based on the average observed noise in copy number segments. Chromosome arms were classified as amplified or deleted if more than 70% of the arm was altered. A sample was considered co-deleted if more than 70% of both 1p and 19q were deleted.

Tumor mutational burden (TMB) is calculated by determining the number of non-synonymous somatic mutations that occur per megabase of exonic sequence data across all genes on the panel. The TMB for a case is reported as a percentile in relation to all prior Profile clinical and research cohort samples sequenced on the current version of Oncopanel, as well as a percentile in relation to all tumors of that specific type.

For Vienna tumor samples, analysis of tumor mutational burden was performed with TruSight Oncology500 provided by illumina platform. Analysis was performed according to manufacturer’s protocol.

#### Multiplexed immunofluorescence and image analysis

FFPE tissue sections were deparaffinized and rehydrated. Antigen retrieval was performed using a pressure cooker and 1x citrate buffer, pH 6.0. Subsequently, sections were stained using the Opal Polaris 7 Color Manual IHC Detection Kit (Akoya Biosciences). Image analysis was performed by using inForm analysis software (Akoya Biosciences) and the open-source software for digital pathology image analysis QuPath.
