#### CD162 detection from tumor tissue via FACS

Tumor samples were placed in PBS and mechanically cut and dissociated into single cell suspensions. Enzymatic dissociation interferes with CD162 protein stability and leads to its degradation. Cell suspension was filtered with a 70uM filter to remove cell clumps. Fc receptor blocking was performed on the total cell suspension using Human TruStain FcX reagent (Biolegend; San Diego, CA). Cell suspensions (1% BSA in PBS) were subsequently stained for cell sorting using the following antibody panels: CD3-APC (Biolegend, 300312) as T cell marker, CD45-FITC (Biolegend, 304006) as marker for Myeloid cells, and CD64-PE (Biolegend, 305008) as exclusion marker to distinguish T cells more specific from other cells, CD162-PeCy7 (Biolegend, 328816) and PD1-BV421 (Biolegend, 329920). As cell viability dye, Zombie NIR was used (Biolegend, 423106). For all experiments, compensation was performed. We used a BD Biosciences Aria III or Sony MA900 fluorescence-activated cell sorter (FACS) with a 100 μm nozzle.

### Quantification and statistical analysis

All computational analyses were performed in R v4.1.0 or Python 3.7.12.

#### Processing of spatial transcriptomics data generated via Xenium

#### Preprocessing of data

The preprocessing of Xenium platform data was conducted using the Seurat pipeline. Initially, the per-transcript location data, cell x gene matrix, cell segmentation, and cell centroid information provided in the Xenium outputs were imported using the LoadXenium function. Subsequently, SCTransform was employed for normalization, followed by standard procedures for dimensionality reduction and clustering.

#### Cell assignment

To assign the sequenced cells an identity, we first clustered cells using Louvain’s algorithm and found clusters for resolutions between 0.1 and 1 with an increment of 0.1. We used SeuratWrappers’s RunPrestoAll function to identify genes that were differentially expressed. We only considered genes detected in at least 10% of the cells within each cluster and showed a mean log difference of at least 0.25. We applied the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Bonferroni correction for multiple testing and only kept genes with an adjusted P-value less than 0.05. For each resolution, the clusters' scores were calculated individually and correlated with the scores of the programs defined in the base and custom panels. Finally, we manually assigned cell identities based on similarities. To confirm the correct cell assignment, we confirmed expression of malignant metaprogram and/or non-malignant cell type marker genes.

#### scRNA-seq data processing and quality control (SMART-Seq2 and 10X genomics)

For smart-seq2, sequencing data was processed from raw reads to gene expression matrices as previously described.18 Briefly, bcl2fastq (v2.20.0) was used to generate demultiplexed FASTQ files and aligned to the human transcriptome (hg19) using hisat263 (v2.1.0). Gene expression levels were quantified using RSEM64(v1.3.0) in paired-end mode, generating transcripts per million (TPM) values.

For 10X genomics, sequencing data was processed using the cellranger (v6.1.0) pipeline with default settings. Cellranger mkfastq was used to generate fastq files followed by alignment to the hg19 transcriptome using cellranger count --chemistry SC5P-PE to generate count matrices.

For tumor and immune data from both SS2 and 10X, a gene was considered to be detected if TPM >0. Immune cells with more than 5,000 or less than 500 genes detected were filtered out. The number of housekeeping genes65 was used as an additional QC metric-immune cells with fewer than 20 housekeeping genes detected were removed. Tumor cells with fewer than 2,000 genes detected, or low housekeeping gene expression (<2.5 mean TPM) were removed.

#### Malignant cell detection (Smart-Seq2)

Copy number variations (CNVs) in tumor samples were estimated by computing a moving average of expression using inferCNV (v1.8.1). The presence of CNVs within a sample was determined using hierarchical clustering of the copy-number profiles generated by inferCNV in comparison to a reference dataset of 190 copy-number profiles determined from normal microglia/macrophage and oligodendrocyte populations.34 Malignancy status was confirmed by graph-based clustering comparing clustering distance between patient samples and normal reference samples. All tumors exhibited clear evidence of CNVs in a subset of cells and did not cluster with the normal reference cells.

#### Normalizing and clustering single cell data (Smart-Seq2 and 10X)

Count matrices were normalized to transcripts per million (TPM) prior to input into seurat processing. All graph-based clustering and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) visualization was performed using Seurat (v4.1.0). Filtered cells were log normalized and scaled to 1E5 using NormalizeData. Variable features were identified using FindVariableFeatures using LogVMR dispersion function and ExpMean to identify average expression. Data was centered using ScaleData. Principal component analysis was run using RunPCA (100 PCs). Cells were integrated by sample ID using harmony66 (v0.1.0; theta = 2). Graph-based Louvain clustering was performed on the top 20 PCs using FindClusters (resolution = 0.8 unless otherwise specified) and k-nearest neighbor algorithm set to 20. Gene expression and clusters were visualized on UMAP embedding of the top 20 PCs (min_dist = 0.3, number of neighbors = 30, distance metric = Euclidean). To identify markers in all subsequent analyses, FindAllMarkers was used (test = wilcox; pvalue adjustment = Bonferroni).

#### Scoring gene sets

Single cell level expression scores were computed as described previously.18 Briefly, given a gene set G for an NMF program or reference gene set, a score S was generated to quantify the relative expression of G within each cell i. This was calculated as the mean centered expression CE of genes in G compared to the centered expression of a background gene set bG, determined as the 100 genes with most similar aggregate expression level to each gene in G. The final score for a given cell i and gene set G is calculated as follows:

$$ s ( i ) = C E [ G , i ] ¯ − C E [ b G , i ] ¯ $$

#### Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF; Smart-Seq2 and 10X genomics)

NMF was used to identify transcriptional programs from relative expression, where negative values are converted to zero. We derived NMF programs for immune cells, separately for all major groups of cells: SS2 pediatric myeloid cells, SS2 pediatric T cells, 10X pediatric myeloid cells, and 10X pediatric T cells as well as from published datasets (SS2 adult myeloid cells, Neftel 2019 and Venteicher 2018; SS2 adult T cells, Mathewson 2021). As input into NMF, we selected the top 2000 most variable genes using SelectIntegrationFeatures from Seurat (selection method = vst). Variable genes were selected separately for each sample. A variety of factors were used to run NMF in order to identify the most biologically robust set of programs (method = brunet, nrun = 10). The final selected factors for each run are as follows: 6 factors for SS2 pediatric myeloid cells, 7 factors for SS2 pediatric T cells, 13 factors for 10X pediatric myeloid cells, 9 factors for 10X pediatric T cells, 8 factors for published adult T cells, and 6 factors for published adult myeloid cells. Following program generation by NMF, gene signatures for each program were produced by differential expression (Seurat FindAllMarkers, method = wilcox, pvalue adjustment method = Bonferroni). The top 100 significant genes (p adjusted <0.05) were selected as the program’s signature gene list. For programs with <100 significant genes, all significant genes were used.

#### Program-wise hierarchical clustering

In order to compare sets of programs, a Pearson correlation and hierarchical clustering approach was used throughout the analysis. For a set of programs, scores were derived as described in the section above (see “scoring gene sets”). Pairwise correlation was performed for each possible pair of programs. These correlation values were then normalized (1 - correlation value) and hierarchically clustered using the R package hclust (method = ward.D2). All correlation heatmaps (Figure S2A, S2C, S4D, S4E, and S5G) show unnormalized Pearson correlation values, ordered by hierarchical clustering values.

#### Projecting annotations from reference dataset

To annotate our anti-PD1 treated scRNA-seq immune cells, we made use of our de novo programs generated from the full ITN cohort. To accomplish this, we used seurat’s FindTransferAnchors function (reduction = pcaproject, normalization.method = LogNormalize, npcs = 40, k.anchor = 5, k.filter = 200, k.score = 30, max.features = 200, n.trees = 50) followed by TransferData (weight.reduction = pcaproject, k.weight = 50, n.trees = 50). This approach was also used for tumor cell annotation (see “tumor cell processing and annotation”). In all instances where this projection method was used, we validated projected annotations by checking expression of expected marker genes.

#### Identification of major immune cell types

While cells were sorted for T cells and myeloid cells, to ensure that our cell populations actually consisted of these cell types based on marker gene expression, cells were computationally annotated as T cell or myeloid. We performed an initial round of graph-based clustering (see “normalizing and clustering single cell data”; no harmony integration was performed at this stage) and then annotated clusters broadly as either T cells or myeloid based on expression of CD3G, CD3E, CD3D, and CSF1R (Figure S1B).

#### Smart-Seq2

To identify doublets, mis-annotated cells, or alternative cell populations (e.g., NK, AC) in T cells, NMF was used to generate T cell programs (R package NMF, v0.23.0; brunet method; 10 runs). No potential doublet programs expressing both T cell (CD3G, CD3E, CD3D) in combination with AC (CLU, APOE) or Myeloid (CSF1R) were identified.

#### 10X gGenomics

Following cluster annotation, cells were split into T cell and Myeloid Seurat objects and clustered as described above, with harmony integration. Expected marker gene (CSF1R, CD3G, CD3D, CD3E) expression was used to validate correct annotation. No cells required corrected annotation.

#### Myeloid cell program identification

#### Smart-Seq2

NMF programs were generated for pediatric myeloid cells using 6 factors, as described above (See nonnegative matrix factorization). To support annotation, program-wise correlation and hierarchical clustering was performed comparing these de novo programs to a set of published myeloid cell states from Antunes et al.27 De novo programs with a high Pearson correlation (≥0.8) to published programs were annotated accordingly.

Using the same adult dataset from Pombo Antunes et al.,27 high-level cell type marker genes were generated (Mo-TAM, Mg-TAM, and monocytes). First, 10X cells were assigned as either Mg-TAM, Mo-TAM, Monocyte, (as defined by Pombo Antunes et al.). Second, markers for these cell types were generated using Seurat’s FindAllMarkers (wilcox test). Finally, pediatric myeloid cells were scored for these genesets (see “scoring gene sets”) and assigned to their max scoring program (Figures 2C and S2F).

We compared our pediatric myeloid cohort to two published adult tumor-associated myeloid cell SS2 datasets.23,24 NMF programs were generated from this merged dataset as described (see “nonnegative matrix factorization”), using rank six. Program-wise hierarchical clustering was performed with these merged programs and our de novo pediatric myeloid programs in order to determine programs that were found in both age groups. Additionally, adult myeloid programs with a high correlation (pearson correlation ≥0.5) with a pediatric myeloid program were annotated accordingly (Figure S2A). Two adult NMF programs (NMF2 and NMF4) had a low correlation with any pediatric myeloid program and were annotated by correlation with the Antunes et al. programs (Figure S4E).

Program annotations were confirmed via GO term overrepresentation analysis using the R package clusterProfiler (v4.0.5; Table S12). Changes in program proportion were assessed for significance using the propeller test from the speckle R package (v1.2.0).

#### 10X genomics

NMF programs were generated for myeloid cells as described (see “nonnegative matrix factorization”) using rank 13. For Hypoxic_TAMs, Microglia, and Monocytes, 2 programs were identified. For Inflammatory, 3 programs were identified. These programs showed high correlation with one another and were merged for downstream analysis (Figures S4C and S4D) for a total of 7 programs.

#### T cell program identification

#### Smart-Seq2

NMF rank eight (see “nonnegative matrix factorization”) was run separately for pediatric T cells as well as a published cohort of adult T cells.5 For the pediatric population, one program was dropped automatically by NMF. Program-wise correlation and hierarchical clustering was performed for the pediatric and adult de novo programs. Genesets for programs that showed clear correlation between adult and pediatric (“shared” programs; pearson correlation >0.6) were merged by union. Genesets that were not shared (“specific” programs) were kept separate. After merging shared genesets, all T cells were scored again for the nine updated gene sets (see “scoring gene sets”). Cells were then assigned to their max scoring program. To not bias the analysis toward “shared” program gene sets (which were substantially larger than “specific” programs due to the union merge), genesets were regenerated using Seurat’s FindAllMarkers (Wilcoxon Rank-Sum test, pvalue adjustment Bonferroni).

T cell programs were annotated primarily based on literature review of marker gene expression. In addition, CD8 programs were also compared to published CD8+ T cell states in other tumor types. Published gene sets reviewed by van der Leun et al. 2020 were compiled into naive, cytotoxic, predysfunctional, and dysfunctional gene sets by selecting genes that were common across multiple tumor types (defined as occurring in ≥ 2 tumor types). Glioma CD8+ cells were scored for these genesets and compared to NMF annotations (Table S14).

#### 10X

NMF rank 9 (see “nonnegative matrix factorization”) was run for 10X genomics T cells. Program-wise correlation and hierarchical clustering was used to confirm high similarity with SS2 programs.

#### Annotation of CD4 and CD8 T cells (SS2 and 10X)

To not bias the NMF analysis due to incorrect CD4/CD8 annotation, NMF was run prior to CD4/CD8 annotation as described above.

After generating nine T cell programs, each program (for adult and pediatric together) was sub-clustered using graph-based clustering (see “normalizing and clustering single cell data”). Four programs- Tregs, cytotoxic, predysfunctional, cytotoxic_Alt (identified in 10X only)- were clearly present exclusively in CD4 or CD8 cells and were annotated without relying on subclusters. For the remaining programs, cells were re-clustered using the same Seurat processing pipeline. Sub-clusters for each program were then annotated as CD4 or CD8 based on expression of CD4, CD8A, and CD8B. CD4+ and CD8+ cells were then re-combined into separate objects and re-clustered.

Because the original scoring and annotation approach involves centering the data around all T cells, the presence of CD4 with CD8 may affect the scoring for CD4 (and vice versa). To address this, CD4 and CD8 cells were normalized and scored separately. Cells were assigned to their max scoring programs and these annotations used for all downstream analyses. Changes in program proportion between pediatric and adult T cells were statistically assessed using the propeller function from the speckle package (v1.2.0).

#### Tumor cell processing and annotation

The tumor cell cohort consists of 23 samples, including 6 previously published samples (EPN_P3, EPN_P6) from Gojo et al., 2020; H3K27M_P1, H3K27M_P2, H3K27M_P3, H3K27M_P4, and H3K27M_P6 from Liu et al., 2022; note that samples were renamed within this cohort to simplify and de-identify; IDs vary from previously published cohorts) as well as 17 unpublished tumor samples. Processing, quality control, and removal of normal cells for tumor cell single cell RNAseq (Smart-Seq2) data was performed as described above (see “scRNA-seq data processing and quality control”). Tumor cell types were annotated separately for ependymoma, GBM, DHG HG34-mutant midline histone WT, and DMG K27M. Unless otherwise specified, harmony was used to integrate within subtypes based on sample as described above (see “normalizing and clustering single cell data”).

For ependymoma tumors, 2/8 patients were included in a previously published cohort and the published annotations were used.18 For the remaining 6 patient samples, previously published PF ependymoma data was used to project annotations to these additional 2 tumors,18 as described above (see “projecting annotations from reference dataset”) and validated using expression of expected genes (Table S10).

For DMG K27M tumors, the resolution parameter for FindClusters was reduced to 0.5. Clusters were annotated by 1) comparing gene overlaps with published K27M programs (fisher’s exact test, p < 0.1; Table S11, tumor_programs_reference_marker_genes.csv) and 2) AddModuleScore (mean score >0.2.34; Higher granularity OPC-like programs (OPC-like-1/-2/-3) were identified as described in Liu et al. 2022,2 but these programs were merged into a single OPC-like program prior to CellChat and co-occurrence analyses.

For GBM tumors, GBM_P2 and GBM_P3 were annotated separately due to poor integration following harmony integration. Cell types were annotated based on mapping graph-based clustering (resolution = 0.8) to published GBM programs (cycling, AC-like, OPC-like programs; Table S11) as well as over-representation of Gene Ontology terms (Neuronal-like, RiboActive programs; data not shown).

For G34 R/V tumors, cells were scored for recently published G34 R/V programs and assigned to their max scoring program, as described above (see “scoring gene sets”; Table S10, tumor_programs_reference_marker_genes.csv).

#### Survival analysis

Bulk RNAseq was downloaded from the cPedBio data portal.67,68 Samples were filtered to retain HGN patients <25 yo. Histone mutation status was assessed by identifying H3F3A mutations in WES data available for all patients.

Deconvolution of bulk data was performed using Cibersort. A single reference was built for all single cell data with cells annotated as either: tumor cells, by CD8 program, by CD4 program, or by Myeloid program. This reference was applied to bulk data and proportions normalized by cell type. For a sample s, program p, and cell type c, normalized proportion NP was calculated as:

$$ N P s , p × N P s , c $$

Kaplan-Meier analysis was run using the R package survival (v3.3-1), splitting samples for each program into “high” (top 50% quantile) and “low” (bottom 50% quantile). Because some programs had a predicted proportion of 0% for many samples, the “high” subset contained fewer than 50% of samples in these cases.

#### Integrated analysis of tumor and immune cells (Smart-Seq2)

#### Co-occurring programs

Pearson correlation was used to test correlation between immune and tumor cell scores on a sample-wise basis. Significant correlation was determined using linear regression. Matching tumor cell types across different tumors had varying genesets (e.g., AC-like in K27M and G34 R/V). To address this, new markers were first generated for all tumor cell types simultaneously using Seurat’s FindAllMarkers (Wilcoxon Rank-Sum test). Tumor cells were then rescored for these markers prior to sample-wise correlation with immune program scores.

#### CellChat

Because CellChat33 (v1.1.0) penalizes ligand/receptor interactions that are not specific to a single pair of cell types/programs, CellChat was used to probe for interactions iteratively between pairs of programs. (CellChat settings: PCthresh = 0.2; population.size = FALSE, min.cells = 10). COL, HLA, LAMININ, and MHC-I pathways were excluded from analysis. Interactions were considered significant if p < 0.05 and probability! = 0. Sankey plots generated using ggalluvial (v0.12.3).

#### Comparison to other tumor types

Publicly available Smart-Seq2 single cell datasets were download25,69 and Seurat objects processed as described in section above (see “normalizing and clustering single cell data”). For melanoma, this metadata was not available and cells were instead annotated as CD4/CD8 on an individual cell level by expression of CD4, CD8A, and CD8B, as described in Tirosh et al. 2016.25 Both datasets were subset to CD8+ T cells before merging with pediatric and adult5 glioma CD8 T cells and integrated by sample using harmony. Cells were scored for CD8 gene sets from Pombo Antunes et al. 2021 (see “scoring gene sets”). Cells were assigned to their max scoring program and markers regenerated using seurat’s FindAllMarkers (Wilcox test) for the 3 tumor types and 4 genesets separately. All CD8 cells were scored for these 12 programs and correlated using Pearson correlation and hierarchical clustering (Figure S6B; see “program-wise hierarchical clustering”).

#### Clonal T cell identification

#### Smart-Seq2

For pediatric T cells, we computationally reconstructed the TCR alpha and beta chain sequences using TraCer70 v0.6.0, Python 3.5.1; Trinity settings: inchworm_only = True, trinity_kmer_length = 17). Tcells were classified as having a reconstructed TCR if productive sequences were reconstructed for alpha and/or beta chains. Clonotypes were defined based on T cells that share an identical alpha and/or beta chain. On average, 4.5 clonotypes (≥ 2 identical TCRs) were identified per sample.

#### 10X genomics

VDJ data from 10X Genomics was processed using cellranger multi (reference: GRCh38; v 6.1.0). Fastqs were first generated for both GEX and VDJ data as described (see “scRNA-seq data processing and quality control”) and used as input for cellranger multi. 10X recommends using cellranger multi over cellranger vdj when both GEX and VDJ data are available for improved T cell calling.

#### Clonal T cell analysis

To test for changes in expression between clonal and non-clonal T cells, we replicated the method in Mathewson et al. 2021 (Figures 5C, S5F, and S5I). Briefly, within each patient, every clonotype was matched to a randomly selected non-clonal T cells drawn from that same patient. Mean expression for each gene in clonal cells was subtracted from mean expression in nonclonal cells. L1 distance was calculated for each gene within all possible combinations of cells within a clonotype and then average. CV was calculated by dividing this mean L1 distance by mean expression across all clonotypes. CV was calculated in the same way for the random sets of non-clonal. Final variability metrics for each gene was calculated as the difference in CV between clonal and nonclonal.

We then generated a background distribution by randomly shuffling expression values between clonal/nonclonal cells for each gene and then calculating the mean expression and CV for this shuffled data in the same way as described above. We repeated this for 100 iterations and then calculated a Z score to compare this background distribution to the observed expression and CV.

To identify significant enrichment of shared clonotypes between paired programs (Figures 5B and S5E) we first identified the number of identical clonotypes found in each pair of programs and then normalized by dividing by the minimum number of unique clonotypes found in the pair in order to control for differences in program size. For a program pair with the set of unique clonotypes in each program p c 1 , p c 2 , this is calculated as:

$$ | p c 1 ∩ p c 2 | m i n i m u m ( | p c 1 | , | p c 2 | ) $$

Permutation testing was used to identify pairs with significant enrichment by randomly assigning program labels and calculating clonotype enrichment as above for 1000 permutations.

To compare the percentage of clonally expanded cells between pediatric and adult tumor-infiltrating T cells, a student’s t.test using the R function t.test from the stats package (v3.5) was performed.

#### Prioritization of putative targets

We performed a coexpression analysis to identify genes that are regulated similarly to cytotoxic CD8+ T cell genes. To accomplish this, we first scored cells for all of our T cell programs (See “scoring gene sets”). As our input gene set, we then filtered to genes with >100 counts across all CD8+ T cells (15,002 genes). We then correlated cell-wise values for each individual gene with each of our CD8+ T cell programs using pearson correlation. We then ordered correlation values for each gene across all programs and assigned each gene a rank for each program (Table S12). Finally, we examined the resulting prioritized gene list for 1) genes that had a high rank in the cytotoxic program but not in all programs (i.e., was somewhat specific to the cytotoxic program) and 2) was described in the literature as a potential targetable exhaustion marker. SELPLG fit both of these criteria.

#### Analysis of ani-PD1 treated tumors

Separately for each sequencing method (SS2 or 10X), PD1-treated pediatric glioma cells were annotated as CD4, CD8, or myeloid based on two metrics: score for projected annotations from the full Smart-Seq2 ITN cohort (see “projecting annotations from reference dataset”; n = 22) as well as manual correction of these projected annotations based on expression of marker genes CD8A, CD8B, and CD4.

Clustering and harmony integration as described previously was performed separately for CD4, CD8, and myeloid cells based on sequencing type (all GBM SS2 samples and all GBM 10X samples, regardless of treatment type). Program annotations from the full SS2 cohort were projected onto these Seurat objects, as described above (see “projecting annotations from reference dataset”). Thus, the program annotations and proportions were generated separately for SS2 and 10X antiPD1-treated samples in order to allow for semi-independent confirmation of results.

Published scRNA-seq data from adult glioma and melanoma anti-PD1-treated samples49,71 were processed as described above (see “normalizing and clustering single cell data”) and annotated as myeloid or T cells based on published annotations. Adult glioma CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were annotated cell-wise based on CD4/CD8 expression as described in Cloughesy et al.49 Any T cells that expressed neither CD4/CD8A or expressed CD4/CD8A equally were removed. ## Abstract

The estrogen receptor-α (ER) drives 75% of breast cancers. On activation, the ER recruits and assembles a 1–2 MDa transcriptionally active complex. These complexes can modulate tumour growth, and understanding the roles of individual proteins within these complexes can help identify new therapeutic targets. Here, we present the discovery of ER and ZMIZ1 within the same multi-protein assembly by quantitative proteomics, and validated by proximity ligation assay. We characterise ZMIZ1 function by demonstrating a significant decrease in the proliferation of ER-positive cancer cell lines. To establish a role for the ER-ZMIZ1 interaction, we measured the transcriptional changes in the estrogen response post-ZMIZ1 knockdown using an RNA-seq time-course over 24 h. Gene set enrichment analysis of the ZMIZ1-knockdown data identified a specific delay in the response of estradiol-induced cell cycle genes. Integration of ENCODE data with our RNA-seq results identified that ER and ZMIZ1 both bind the promoter of E2F2. We therefore propose that ER and ZMIZ1 interact to enable the efficient estrogenic response at subset of cell cycle genes via a novel ZMIZ1–ER–E2F2 signalling axis. Finally, we show that high ZMIZ1 expression is predictive of worse patient outcome, ER and ZMIZ1 are co-expressed in breast cancer patients in TCGA and METABRIC, and the proteins are co-localised within the nuclei of tumour cell in patient biopsies. In conclusion, we establish that ZMIZ1 is a regulator of the estrogenic cell cycle response and provide evidence of the biological importance of the ER–ZMIZ1 interaction in ER-positive patient tumours, supporting potential clinical relevance.

## Introduction

Approximately 75% of breast cancers are classified as estrogen receptor-α (ER) positive. In these cancers, the ER is no longer correctly regulated, subverts cell division regulation, and becomes the driving transcription factor in the tumour (Mohammed et al. 2013). Only a few primary breast cancers have mutations in the ER (Oesterreich & Davidson 2013), yet the transcriptional activity is frequently abnormal (Carroll 2016). In many metastatic tumours, the ER is still active and drives the growth of the tumour with a reduced dependence on estrogen or in a ligand-independent manner (Robinson et al. 2013, Toy et al. 2013). This critical role for the ER in disease progression has therefore made the protein a key target for therapeutics such as fulvestrant (Osborne et al. 2004) and tamoxifen (Jordan 2003). More recently, tamoxifen has been prescribed as a preventative treatment in high-risk healthy patients to successfully reduce their chances of developing breast cancer (Cuzick et al. 2015). Most women benefit from endocrine therapy with 50–70% of cases responding to treatment. However, relapse is common with the risk ranging from 10% to 41% (Pan et al. 2017).

## The ER transcriptional complex

One strategy to overcome relapse focuses on protein that function with or alter the transcriptional response of the ER to estrogen. The majority of ER-binding sites are at distal enhancer elements (Carroll et al. 2005). On binding to these sites, the receptor catalyses the formation of chromatin loops and recruits a wide range of proteins along with the mediator complex to form complexes up to 1–2 MDa in size (Liu et al. 2014). Through these interactions, the ER is able to facilitate the activation of RNA polymerase II at the promoters of target genes (Murakami et al. 2017). Without the coordination of the ER and the formation of these complexes, it is not possible for the efficient transcription of target genes to occur.

Further characterisation of ER-interacting proteins is therefore essential to identify targets for novel treatment strategies. Successful examples of cofactorbased approaches include studies demonstrating that the GREB1–ER–EZH2 transcriptional axis is directly involved in tamoxifen resistance (Wu et al. 2018) or identifying the pioneer-factor FOXA1 as a key opportunity for future interventions (Nakshatri & Badve 2007, Behan et al. 2019).

This study aims to lay the groundwork for future targeted therapies by presenting proteomic and genomic evidence that ZMIZ1 is co-expressed with ER in patient tumours and that the inhibition in ZMIZ1 reduces the early transcriptional response of cell cycle genes to

estrogen in ER-positive breast cancer cells via a novel ZMIZ1–ER–E2F2 signalling axis.

## Materials and methods

## Cell lines and general cell culture

MCF7, T47D (ER-positive cell lines) and MDA-MB-231 (ER-negative cell lines) were obtained from ATCC. All cells were routinely cultured in DMEM with high glucose and pyruvate (Gibco, 41966-029) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS). Cells were confirmed to be mycoplasma-free using the MycoStrip test supplied by InvivoGen. Cell line authentication was confirmed by short tandem repeat genetic profiling carried out by Eurofins. All cell lines were used at less than 35 passages for all experimental work described below.

## Quantitative multiPLEXed rapid immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry of endogenous proteins

Quantitative multiPLEXed rapid immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry of endogenous proteins (qPLEX- RIME) samples were prepared as previously reported (Papachristou et al. 2018). Cells were grown in estrogenfree culture as previously described (Guertin et al. 2018). In summary, cells were cultured for 4 days in phenol red-free DMEM (Gibco) with 10% charcoal-stripped FBS and glutamine, cells were washed with PBS and media was changed daily to remove residual estrogen. Cells were cross-linked for qPLEX-RIME 45 min after the addition of 100 nM estradiol (E2) (Sigma-Aldrich) or vehicle control (ethanol).

## Proximity ligation assay

Cell lines were seeded into eight-well chamber slides in estrogen-rich complete media (DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and glutamine), as previously described by Mohammed et al. (2015). After 48 h (around 50% confluence) cells were treated with 100 nM fulvestrant (Cayman 10011269) or vehicle control (ethanol). For knockdown experiments, cells were transfected using a reverse siRNA transfection with Lipofectamine RNAiMAX Transfection Reagent (Invitrogen, 13778075) and the SMARTpool on-target siZMIZ1 siRNAs along with the matched siCTRL (Dharmacon). After 24 h of treatment with fulvestrant or 48 h with siRNA, cells were rinsed in PBS and fixed with ice-cold methanol. The PLA assay (Sigma-Aldrich) was then performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions with anti-ER antibody supplied by Abcam (Ab3575) diluted at 1:400 and anti-ZMIZ1 supplied by Santa Cruz (SC-376825) diluted at 1:250. ## Cell growth assay

MCF7, T47D, and MDA-MB-231 cell growth was undertaken in estrogen-rich complete media with 10% FBS and glutamine, monitored by incucyte. siRNA knockdown was undertaken with SMARTpool on-target siZMIZ1 siRNAs along with the matched siCTRL (Dharmacon) and was transfected with Lipofectamine RNAiMAX reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Cells were reverse transfected, and media was refreshed after 24 h to minimise the toxicity of the transfection reagents.

Knockdown was confirmed by RT-qPCR and western blotting.

## Western blotting of ZMIZ1

Western blotting was performed in accordance with the General Protocol for Western Blotting provided by Bio-Rad with certain modifications. SDS-PAGE was carried out using 4–20% Mini-PROTEAN® TGX™ Precast Gels from Bio-Rad. Proteins were transferred from the gel to a PVDF membrane in the iBlot 2 Transfer Stacks (Thermo Fisher, IB24001) using the iBlot 2 Gel Transfer Device.

Five percent (w/v) fat-free milk in TBST buffer was used as the blocking buffer. Primary and secondary antibodies were appropriately diluted using the blocking buffer. Antibodies were as follows: RAI17/ZMIZ1 (E2X3X, 1:1000) rabbit mAb (Cell Signaling Technology, 89500), anti-b-Actin antibody (Sigma A1978, 1:5000), peroxidase AffiniPure goat anti-rabbit IgG (Jackson ImmnuoResearch 111-035-144, 1:7500), peroxidase AffiniPure goat anti-mouse IgG (Jackson ImmnuoResearch 115-035-174, 1:7500). Chemiluminescent imaging was performed using SuperSignal West Pico PLUS Chemiluminescent Substrate (Thermo Fisher, 34579) with an iBright imaging system (Thermo Fisher).

## RNA-sequencing and GSEA

Cell growth was undertaken in phenol red-free DMEM + 10% charcoal-stripped FBS. siRNA knockdown was undertaken with SMARTpool ontarget siZMIZ1 along with the matched siCTRL (Dharmacon) and was transfected with Lipofectamine RNAiMAX reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific). About 24 h after transfection, the media was refreshed, and stimulated with 100 nM E2 or vehicle control. After 3, 6, 12 and 24 h stimulation with either E2 or ethanol, RNA was collected for four biological replicates per cell line and libraries were prepared by TruSeq mRNA Library Prep (Illumina). The libraries were sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq 4000 platform. Reads were aligned with HiSat2 to hg19 and count matrix established with HtseqCount v2.1.0. Differential analysis of expression was undertaken with the R-package DESeq2 (Love et al. 2014) and GSEA (Mootha et al. 2003, Subramanian et al. 2005) was undertaken using the implementation in VULCAN (Holding et al. 2019).

## Chromatin immunoprecipitation–quantitative real-time PCR

## Results

## qPLEX-RIME of ER activation identifies novel co-factor ZMIZ1

We used qPLEX-RIME, a state-of-the-art method for quantifying protein–protein interactions within nuclear receptor complexes (Papachristou et al. 2018), to quantitatively monitor the changes in protein–protein interactions in the ER complex between 0 and 45 min in response to activating MCF7 cells (ER-positive cell line) with estradiol (Fig. 1A). The assay was repeated across four isogenic replicates.

Detected protein–ER interactions that were found to significantly change on stimulation with estradiol (P < 0.05) and had a two-fold change in protein intensity were reviewed for known biology. We found several previously identified ER co-factors including

RARA, CBP, EP300, NRIP1 and GATA3. We also detected SUMO1-3 within the ER complex, most likely as a result of the covalent modification of the ER-α or another protein within the ER chromatin-bound complex, in agreement with previous ChIP-seq experiments (Traboulsi et al. 2018). In addition, we found novel putative ER interactions within the data (Fig. 1B and Supplementary Table 1).

The list of potential new ER co-factors includes ZMIZ1 (Fig. 1C), which had previously been identified as a co-activator of the androgen receptor (AR) (Li et al. 2011, Sharma et al. 2003). However, a key result of that study is that the effect was AR-specific in CV-1 cells. Transfection of ZMIZ1 into CV-1 cells was not able to enhance glucocorticoid receptor, progesterone receptor, ER, and vitamin D receptor-mediated transcription (Sharma et al. 2003). The AR specificity of the previous ZMIZ1 result has since been incorporated in the GeneCards and UniProt databases (UniProt Consortium 2019) and unpublished yeast data, discussed by Sharma et al. (2003), supports the literature that there is no interaction between ZMIZ1 and non-AR nuclear receptors. Given that our qPLEX-RIME data shows a significant enrichment of ZMIZ1 protein vs the control, was undertaken using a breast cancer cell line, and that we did not detect the presence of AR in our qPLEX- RIME data, this implies AR was not within the ER complex in the experimental conditions used. Therefore, we considered the breast cancer specific function of ZMIZ1 to be of key interest for follow-up studies.

Proximity ligation assay confirms that the ZMIZ1 and ER proteins are within 40 nm in ER-positive cell lines

We applied PLA to validate our qPLEX-RIME results. To confirm the specificity of the signal to ER protein, we conducted an ER–ER PLA. The results showed a significant reduction in PLA signal in both MCF7 and T47D cells, confirming the specificity of our antibodies to the ER protein. ## ZMIZ1 and ER co-bind and co-regulate cell cycle regulator E2F2

As ZMIZ1 and ER are both found in DNA-binding complexes, we aimed to establish if the proteins were bound in proximity of the same DNA elements that

regulate cell cycle. We surmised that any sites we identified could indicate a potential cell cycle regulatory mechanism involving both ER and ZMIZ1 proteins. For ZMIZ1 binding, we used the ENCODE data reported in K562 cells, as no data for MCF7 cells was available, and for ER binding, we used data as reported by ENCODE in MCF7 cells (Luo et al. 2020). Overlaying these data demonstrated that nearly 10% of ZMIZ1, 1094 sites in total, were found to also bind ER (Fig. 3D) in support of our PLA results. Comparison of the overlap in ER and ZMIZ1-binding sites with our GSEA gene set identified E2F2 as being within both data sets (Fig. 3A). ENCODE reported two binding sites that passed their QC pipeline within the E2F2 gene loci for both ER and ZMIZ1, and both sites overlapped. Visual inspection of the ENCODE data showed clear binding of ER and ZMIZ1 at E2F2 promoter region. While the second binding site within the E2F2 intron was clearly bound by ER, the intronic ZMIZ1 ChIP-seq peak was at similar levels to background noise (Fig. 3B). To address concerns that the ENCODE ChIP-seq data was generated in K562 cells and shows poor enrichment over noise, we validated the ZMIZ1 binding of the E2F2 promoter in the MCF7 cell line. Our ChIP-qPCR results confirmed that the ENCODE ZMIZ1 ChIP-seq result was generalisable to our breast cancer model and that degrading ER with fulvestrant led to the loss of ZMIZ1 binding but had no effect on our IgG control ChIP (Fig. 3C). Further analyses of the RNAseq data showed a reduction in E2F2 expression, with a maximum log2fold change of −1.6 at 3 h, and a log2- fold change of −1.4 between 6 and 12 h (Fig. 3E). The Pvalues for the siZMIZ1/siCTRL comparison of the E2F2 transcript as calculated by DESeq2 at the 3-, 6-, 12-, and 24-h time points were P = 0.01, 0.007, 0.007 and 0.5, respectively. Overall, these results indicate a delayed estrogenic expression of the E2F2 transcription factor as a result of the loss of the ZMIZ1 at the E2F2 promoter. We also noted, E2F2 was previously reported as critical for ER-positive breast tumour biology and disease progression (Nguyen-Vu et al. 2013).

## High ZMIZ1 expression correlates with low survival in ER-positive patients

To explore if the role of ZMIZ1 activity held clinical importance, we investigated if ZMIZ1 expression was a predictor of patient survival in the context of both ER-positive and ER-negative breast tumours using KMplot (Lanczky et al. 2016).

Stratifying ER-positive patients (ER status by array) by median ZMIZ1 expression showed that ER-positive patients with higher levels of ZMIZ1 expression had significantly poorer outcome (P = 0.0065, logrank test, hazard ratio (HR) = 1.18 (1.05–1.33)). In contrast, the same analysis of ER-negative patients demonstrated no significant difference in patient outcome (P = 0.38, logrank test, Fig. 5A). Survival differences were also confirmed in METABRIC (Curtis et al. 2012) and TCGA (Weinstein et al. 2013) ER-positive breast cancer cohorts (Supplementary Fig. 14).

Splitting the ER-positive patient cohort into those who received no endocrine therapy and those on tamoxifen only (Fig. 5B) showed that ZMIZ1 expression had no significant effect on the survival of those who received no endocrine therapy (P = 0.27, logrank test, HR = 1.12 (0.92–1.37)). Patients who did receive tamoxifen and who expressed greater than median levels of ZMIZ1 saw a significant reduction in recurrent-free survival (P = 0.0051, logrank test, HR = 1.52 (1.13–2.05)).

These results were consistent with the ZMIZ1 functioning as part of the ER protein complex and that ZMIZ1 plays a role in disease progression in ER-positive breast cancer.

## Immunohistochemistry of ZMIZ1 and ER demonstrates both proteins locate in the same regions of patient tumours

To further validate the link between ER and ZMIZ1, we checked if ZMIZ1 expression was found in the ER-positive tumour cells in clinical material. Visual inspection of ER-positive breast cancer tumours from all three patients analysed showed strong nuclear staining of both proteins in adjacent sections. Comparison of the localisation of staining between ER and ZMIZ1 demonstrated that both proteins were found within the nucleus of epithelial cells. Neither ER nor ZMIZ1 was detected in the infiltrating cells. Further, the distribution of ER and ZMIZ1 staining correlated, implicating that ER and ZMIZ1 are expressed within the same cells of the patient tumours (Fig. 5D).

## ZMIZ1 and marker of proliferation KI67 protein levels significantly correlate in patient tumours

To establish if ZMIZ1 protein abundance correlated with cell proliferation (KI67) rate, we undertook the analysis of the published TCGA quantitative proteomic data (PXD024322) (Asleh et al. 2022). All of ZMIZ1, KI67 and ER protein abundances correlated strongly (P < 0.001, Pearson’s) (Fig. 5E) with each other. The associated R-value showed a higher correlation between ZMIZ1 and KI67 (0.70) than between ER and ZMIZ1 (0.59). The highest correlation was between ER and KI67 (0.78). Partial correlation (Pearson’s) was applied to confirm if ZMIZ1 protein expression had an effect on KI67 protein independent of ER. The correlation between ZMIZ1 and KI67 was significant at 0.46 (P < 4.9 × 10−21)

when controlling for ER protein abundance. For comparison, the correlation of ER to KI67 controlling for ZMIZ1 protein abundance was 0.63 (P < 1.7 × 10−42). Overall, these results confirmed the ZMIZ1 expression correlated with marker of proliferation KI67 significantly and in addition to the ZMIZ1 protein abundance correlating with ER protein expression.

## Discussion

All previous evidence supported the conclusion that ZMIZ1 was an AR-specific co-activator (Sharma et al. 2003). Results in the cited study demonstrated that AR, ER and other steroid hormone receptors could all activate transcription when presented with their respective ligands in the cell line models used. However, only the activity of AR was linked to the levels of ZMIZ1 within the cell. Therefore, on detection of ZMIZ1 within the ER complex in the absence of AR, we hypothesised that the absence of evidence for an ER-ZMIZ1 interaction until this point may be as a result of the cell line models used in previous research.

Undertaking analysis in ER-positive breast cancer cell line models, we demonstrated a significant change in the ER-mediated transcriptional response on ZMIZ1 knockdown. Further, we were able to show that within patient samples where ZMIZ1, ER and KI67 protein expressions correlated, ZMIZ1 expression is predictive of survival, and the proteins are both localised within the nuclei of patient tumour cells. Combined, these results provide good evidence of an important role for ZMIZ1 in ER-positive breast cancer.

Previously, it has been shown that ZMIZ1 has a very strong transactivation domain (TAD) (Sharma et al. 2003) and our findings do not rule out this mechanism. However, in stark contrast to the AR-ZMIZ1 interaction, our research, along with that of other investigators, yielded no definitive evidence of a direct proteinprotein interaction through co-immunoprecipitation. Instead, we have shown the two proteins are in close proximity via PLA and both proteins bind the E2F2 promoter by ChIP-qPCR. An explanation for the discrepancy in our results is that PLA detects proteins within the complex through space, and qPLEX-RIME uses cross-linking to both DNA and protein to capture transient interactions, while native Co-IP is more dependent on the protein−protein affinities within the protein complex. These observations, and the reported results that ZMIZ1 cannot co-activate ER in the original AR-ZMIZ1 interaction studies, suggest that the ER−ZMIZ1 interaction in breast cancer may be via a different mechanism to that in the prostate. One potential alternative is ZMIZ1 may activate the ER by promoting the SUMOylation of either the ER or its co-factors via its SP-RING domain (Li et al. 2011).
